question: An owner of a pizza and Italian foods restaurant opens a new location on a street where another owner has a burger restaurant. It seems like business is slow for the pizza place owner and he eyes up his competitor, the burger man, as the reason. The pizza owner starts to make false statements about the burger restaurant and its inferior ingredients, which he says have been causing ptomaine poisoning in some of the customers. When burger joint owner loses customers and business income to pizza place owner, can he sue for conversion?

options.A: No, because conversion consists of appropriating another's real property.
options.B: No, because the burger owner failed to prove that the pizza owner's statements were false.
options.C: No, because there was no interference with his ownership or right of possession to his personal property.
options.D: No, because the pizza owner has the right to advertise his business as he sees fit.
options.E: No, because the burger owner did not suffer any physical harm or damage to his property.
options.F: Yes, conversion is an intentional tort and the pizza owner acted intentionally to convert and did convert part of the burger business.
options.G: Yes, because the pizza owner committed a tort of defamation, which is a form of conversion.
options.H: Yes, because the pizza owner's actions caused economic harm to the burger owner.
options.I: Yes, because the pizza owner violated the burger owner's right to a fair competition.
options.J: Yes, because the pizza owner interfered with his right of peaceful enjoyment and disrupted his business activities.
